---
title: "The Anatomy of Embedding and Latent Spaces"
subtitle: "From Shannon's Bits to High-Dimensional Geometric Knowledge"
---

In 1948, Claude Shannon defined information as the reduction of uncertainty, measured in bits [@shannon1948mathematical]. His entropy formula turned out to be identical in form to the one Boltzmann and Gibbs had used for thermodynamic systems in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries—a resemblance Shannon himself noted, though it was Edwin T. Jaynes who, in 1957, argued that statistical mechanics is itself a form of inference [@jaynes1957information]. But Shannon drew a deliberate boundary: "[t]hese semantic aspects of communication are irrelevant to the engineering problem." A bit is a unit of uncertainty, not of meaning.

The **Embedding Revolution** is the complement to Shannon's syntactic theory: it represents meaning itself—or at least its statistical shadow—as continuous coordinates on high-dimensional manifolds. Fittingly, it does so using Shannon's own tools: cross-entropy and mutual information are the objectives that shape these spaces.

This chapter lays the foundation for the rest of the book. We start with why discrete, orthogonal representations hit a geometric wall, then examine how latent manifolds are built and what their geometry looks like. We close with the places where a single vector strains: a ledger of limits, each stated as a cost rather than a failure, which the rest of the book examines.

## Shannon's Information Theory

Shannon measured the information of a message by its surprise: a message with probability $p$ carries $-\log_2 p$ bits. Near-certain messages ($p \approx 1$) tell us almost nothing, while rare ones ($p \approx 0$) are highly informative. The *entropy* of a source is the average of this surprisal. For a binary source that emits a one with probability $p$ and a zero with probability $1-p$, it is

$$
H_b(p) = -p \log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p),
$$

which peaks at one bit when $p = 1/2$ and vanishes when the outcome is certain. For a stream of $n$ bits that are independent and identically distributed, entropies add:

$$
H(X_1,\dots,X_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} H(X_i) = n\,H_b(p).
$$

Consider a faulty sensor that outputs a one with probability $p = 0.9$. Seeing a one is unsurprising, while seeing a zero is a rare event:

| $p$ | Surprisal of a one | Surprisal of a zero | Entropy $H_b(p)$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0.50 | 1.000 bits | 1.000 bits | 1.000 bits |
| 0.90 | 0.152 bits | 3.322 bits | 0.469 bits |
| 0.99 | 0.014 bits | 6.644 bits | 0.081 bits |

: Surprisal of each outcome and entropy of a binary source. {#tbl-binary-entropy}

For $p = 0.9$ the average is $H_b(0.9) = 0.9 \times 0.152 + 0.1 \times 3.322 \approx 0.47$ bits per symbol. The zeros are individually informative, but they are so rare that the stream as a whole is highly predictable. A fair coin cannot be compressed, because every flip costs a full bit. The sensor stream can: a log of 1000 symbols can, on average, be squeezed into about 470 bits, and no lossless scheme can do better.


::: {.questions}
1. A sensor emits a one with probability $p = 0.8$ and a zero otherwise, independently at each step. Compute the surprisal of a one and of a zero, the entropy $H_b(0.8)$, and the minimum expected size, in bits, of a lossless encoding of a 10,000-symbol log. How does this compare with a fair coin?

2. A general sends one of two equally likely messages: "attack at dawn" or "attack at dusk". How many bits does each message carry according to Shannon? Now replace "attack at dusk" with the meaningless string "xqzv jwk", keeping its probability fixed. Does the entropy change, and what does this tell you about the relationship between entropy and meaning?
:::


## Shannon's Boundary Problem

Notice what the calculations above needed: the probabilities of the symbols, and nothing else. The sensor could report temperatures, heartbeats or coin flips and its entropy would be the same. Ignoring meaning was not a weakness but the source of the theory's power. Because entropy depends only on probabilities, the same mathematics applies to any source and any channel, and it became foundational across computer science: the compression behind every ZIP, JPEG and MP3, the error-correcting codes in our disks, QR codes and mobile networks, the capacity limits that govern Wi-Fi and fiber, and, through cross-entropy, the loss function that trains modern neural networks. Shannon had already laid the other foundation of computing in his 1937 master's thesis, where he showed that Boolean algebra describes switching circuits [@shannon1937symbolic]. That algebra was George Boole's, from 1854, which he called the laws of thought: symbols that are true or false, combined by AND, OR and NOT, with nothing in between [@boole1854investigation]. Both foundations are discrete: a symbol is this one or that one, and a proposition is true or false. 

However, that indifference to meaning is also the boundary of the theory. The messages "attack at dawn" and "attack at dusk" can have the same probability, and therefore exactly the same information content, yet they mean very different things. A one-bit message has the same entropy whether it says that a coin landed heads or that it is raining today. For Shannon this was a feature: the engineer's job is to deliver the message faithfully through a channel, not to understand it.

His collaborator Warren Weaver made the division explicit in 1949 [@weaver1949recent] by splitting the communication problem into three levels: **A**, the technical problem (how accurately can symbols be transmitted?); **B**, the semantic problem (how precisely do the symbols convey the desired meaning?); and **C**, the effectiveness problem (how well does the received meaning change behaviour?). Shannon solved level A. Embeddings are an attempt at level B, and the techniques that shape what a system does with the meaning it has received, alignment and agents among them, are arguably attempts at level C. This book is about level B: a map of where embeddings sit among the three.

Shannon also showed, in the same 1948 paper, how far statistics alone can go. He generated English-like text by choosing each word according to how often it follows the previous one, and obtained [@shannon1948mathematical]:

> `THE HEAD AND IN FRONTAL ATTACK ON AN ENGLISH WRITER...`

Locally the text is plausible, since each word follows its predecessor with a believable frequency, yet globally it is meaningless. It is a language model in embryo: it has absorbed some of the syntax and none of the semantics. Some seventy years later, the same recipe with vastly more data and a far richer notion of context produced the large language models whose internal vectors we examine in Chapter 4. Shannon himself was wary of the hype that success brought. In "The Bandwagon" (1956) [@shannon1956bandwagon] he warned that information theory had become a fashion, and that borrowing its vocabulary for psychology, biology or linguistics did not make those fields more rigorous. Like relativity and quantum theory, it suffered the fate of successful theories: its words travelled much further than its mathematics. Yet the separation of form from meaning was not Shannon's alone: linguistics reached it independently.

::: {.questions}
1. Take a plain-text book from the Internet (for example, from Project Gutenberg) and compute the probability of each letter. What is the entropy of this distribution, and how does it compare with $\log_2 26$?

2. With the same book, compute the probability of each word. What is its entropy? Where does the difference with the letter entropy come from?

3. Finally, estimate the probability of each word given the previous $n$ words and use it to generate a random phrase. How does the result change as $n$ grows from 1 to 3?
:::

## Chomsky's Staircase: Structure Without Meaning

The same separation between the form of a message and what it means appeared in linguistics within a decade of Shannon's paper. Chomsky classified formal languages by the machine needed to recognize them, and each machine on the staircase adds one kind of memory [@chomsky1956three]. A finite automaton has no memory beyond its current state, so it recognizes the regular languages, whose patterns depend only on a bounded amount of recent history. A pushdown automaton adds a stack, a last-in first-out memory of unbounded size, which is exactly what is needed to match nested structure such as balanced parentheses (push when a bracket opens, pop when it closes), and it recognizes the context-free languages. Linear-bounded automata, which recognize the context-sensitive languages, get a working tape as long as the input, and Turing machines, at the top, get an unbounded tape. The staircase classifies sets of strings, but the same machines can carry probabilities on their transitions: a Markov chain or hidden Markov model is a probabilistic finite automaton, and a probabilistic context-free grammar is its context-free counterpart. The probabilities decide which strings are likely, not what the machine can remember, so the memory of each step stays the same.

Shannon's word-pair text comes from a bigram model, the probabilistic version of the bottom step: a Markov chain in which the previous word alone sets the probabilities of the next. Its only memory is that previous word, so it cannot even remember whether it has opened a parenthesis, and no choice of probabilities changes that. Programming languages sit on two steps at once. Their syntax lives one step up: it is largely context-free, since matching nested brackets and blocks needs a stack, it is written in Backus–Naur form, and parsing it is decidable and fast. Their runtime behaviour, however, sits at the very top, since general-purpose languages are Turing complete. Yet each step adds structure, not meaning. A parser can tell you that `x = y + 1` is well formed, but not what `x` is for. What a program *means* is what it does, and Rice's theorem, which we meet two sections ahead, says that this cannot in general be read off its text.

Natural language is the mirror image: its meaning is rich, but its grammar resists formalization. Both worlds share one design decision: the symbol itself is atomic, an identity with no interior. `dawn` and `dusk` are as different to a parser as `dawn` and `xqzv`. Programmers know this: renaming every variable consistently leaves the behaviour of a program unchanged (known as alpha-equivalence). Natural language is the opposite: replacing one word by another in the same sentence changes what it says ("attack at dawn" is not "attack at dusk"), because each word carries meaning of its own. In a program, whatever meaning a human reads in `customer_balance` was smuggled in by the author. The machine only ever checks for equality, not for meaning.

Linguistics offered only coarse ways out. A tag such as `NOUN` is the lowest-resolution embedding that could be built by hand, a class label that says almost nothing about the word. Parse trees and the Chomsky hierarchy are tree-shaped, a hint that hierarchies will need a geometry of their own (@sec-hyperbolic-spaces). The more radical way out was philosophical: the late Wittgenstein's "meaning is use" and Firth's "you shall know a word by the company it keeps" [@firth1957synopsis] move meaning from the symbol into its context. Statistics can measure context.

Anyone who has searched a database with ``WHERE content LIKE '%monarch%'`` and found no trace of "king" or "queen" has met this wall. Equality is the whole geometry of a symbol table, and the next section shows how poor that geometry is: written as one-hot vectors, every pair of distinct symbols sits at exactly the same distance, $\sqrt{2}$, so `dawn` is no closer to `dusk` than to `xqzv`. Giving symbols an interior, so that distance carries meaning, is what the rest of this chapter is about.

::: {.questions}
1. Write a program that decides whether a string of brackets `()[]{}` is balanced, using a stack.

2. Write a program that decides whether a string belongs to $\{a^n b^n c^n : n \ge 0\}$ (e.g., "aabbcc" belongs to the set, but "aaabbbcc" does not) using no memory other than the input itself: a tape as long as the input, which you may overwrite, and a constant number of variables. Then try to adapt your stack-based solution of the previous question: what goes wrong?

3. Write an interpreter for MiniBrainf***, a tiny Turing-complete language. Its machine is a tape of cells, all starting at 0 and extending without limit to the right, with a head on the first cell. A program is a string of seven instructions, executed in order: `>` and `<` move the head one cell right or left; `+` and `-` add or subtract 1 from the current cell; `.` prints the current cell; `[` jumps forward to the matching `]` if the current cell is 0; `]` jumps back to the matching `[` if the current cell is not 0. Run `++++++++[>++++++++<-]>+.`, then run `+[>+]` and `+[]` with a limit on the number of steps. Why can no linear-bounded automaton do what your interpreter does?
:::

## The Orthogonal Catastrophe: Why Symbolic Tables Hit a Geometric Wall

The Chomsky staircase has a hidden feature: it only climbs in one direction. Each step gives the machine more memory, from a bare state to a stack, a bounded tape and an unbounded tape, but all four steps rest on the same flat floor, the alphabet. A finite automaton decides what to do next by looking up its current state and the symbol it just read in a transition table. A pushdown automaton pushes and pops symbols and checks whether the top one is the one it expects. A Turing machine reads and writes symbols on its tape. In every case the only question a machine can ask about two symbols is whether they are the same. The staircase measures how much *structure* a machine can keep track of, and says nothing about how much *meaning* its symbols carry, because as far as the machine is concerned they carry none. We will call this the **orthogonal catastrophe**: a hierarchy of rich structure built on symbols that have no geometry, because, as we will see, every symbol sits at a right angle to every other and equally far from all of them.

To see the catastrophe we need to write symbols as numbers, since computers can only process numbers. The standard trick, known in machine learning jargon as **one-hot encoding**, is the following. Fix an ordering of the vocabulary $V$, a list of $|V|$ distinct symbols. The $j$-th symbol is represented by a vector with $|V|$ entries, all equal to 0 except for a single 1 in position $j$ (the "hot" entry). Take a toy vocabulary of five words:

| Word | Vector | $i=1$ | $i=2$ | $i=3$ | $i=4$ | $i=5$ |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `dawn` | $\mathbf{e}_1$ | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `dusk` | $\mathbf{e}_2$ | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `king` | $\mathbf{e}_3$ | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| `queen` | $\mathbf{e}_4$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| `xqzv` | $\mathbf{e}_5$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

: One-hot encoding of a five-word vocabulary. Each row is the vector $\mathbf{e}_j \in \mathbb{R}^5$ of a word, and the column $i$ gives its $i$-th entry, $(\mathbf{e}_j)_i = 1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise. {#tbl-one-hot}

A one-hot vector is just the position of a word in the vocabulary, written as a vector instead of as a number: the word is its index, and the index is the word, like the line number of an entry in a dictionary. It is also how the bottom step of the staircase looks in linear algebra. If the state of a finite automaton is written as a one-hot vector, reading a symbol is multiplying it by a matrix of zeros and ones that moves the single 1 to the next state. A probabilistic automaton uses a matrix of probabilities instead, and Shannon's bigram model is the same idea: multiplying a one-hot vector for the previous word by a table of next-word probabilities selects one row, the distribution of what comes next. In all these cases the one-hot vector acts as a pointer into a transition table, a matrix.

Multiplying by a matrix is one thing we can do with a one-hot vector; the other is to compare it with a second vector. The natural way to turn a pair of vectors into a single number is the **dot product**, $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \sum_k u_k v_k$: multiply the two vectors entry by entry and add the results. Each position in which both vectors are large contributes to the sum, so the dot product measures how much they have in common. Two vectors with dot product zero are **orthogonal**, which geometrically means that they form a right angle, and informally that they share nothing: no position is active in both. For one-hot vectors, the dot product with $\mathbf{e}_i$ selects the $i$-th entry of the other vector, $\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{v} \rangle = v_i$, and when $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{e}_j$ that entry is 1 only if the two words are the same, so the dot product is a test for equality,

$$
\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j \rangle = \delta_{ij} =
\begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{if } i \neq j, \end{cases}
$$

where $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta. Distances follow immediately. Expanding the squared norm of the difference and using $\|\mathbf{e}_i\| = 1$,

$$
\|\mathbf{e}_i - \mathbf{e}_j\|_2^2 = \|\mathbf{e}_i\|^2 + \|\mathbf{e}_j\|^2 - 2\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j \rangle = 1 + 1 - 0 = 2,
$$

so $\|\mathbf{e}_i - \mathbf{e}_j\|_2 = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$ for *every* pair of distinct words. In the toy vocabulary, `dawn` is exactly as far from `dusk` as from `xqzv`, and `king` is as far from `queen` as from `dawn`. The cosine similarity, which measures the angle, is 0 for every pair of distinct words as well. Whether we measure the distance between two words or their cosine similarity, the answer to "how similar are these two words?" is the same for all pairs, $\sqrt{2}$ in one case and 0 in the other, and therefore uninformative.

::: {.questions}
1. A finite automaton accepts the binary strings with an even number of 1s. Write its state as a one-hot vector of length 2 (even, odd) and give a $2 \times 2$ matrix to each input symbol, so that reading a symbol is a matrix–vector product. Check the result against the parity of the 1s on all strings of up to 10 symbols. What do the columns of these matrices look like, and how would they change for a probabilistic automaton?

2. Consider a logistic regression without bias, $p = \sigma(\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle)$ with $\sigma(t) = 1/(1+e^{-t})$, trained on examples $(\mathbf{x}, y)$ with $y \in \{0, 1\}$ to minimize the cross-entropy loss $L = -y \ln p - (1-y)\ln(1-p)$. Derive the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L$ and write the gradient descent update of $\mathbf{w}$ with learning rate $\eta$. Which weights change when $\mathbf{x}$ is a one-hot vector? Then train the model to label `dawn` as 1 ("is a time of day") and `king` and `queen` as 0, twice: with one-hot inputs, and with the hand-made dense vectors of the table below, whose values are illustrative and not learned (`xqzv` gets a small noise vector). What probability does each model assign to `dusk`, which it never saw during training, and to `xqzv`?

   | Word | time of day | person | royal | male | brightness |
   |:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
   | `dawn` | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0.4 |
   | `dusk` | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | $-0.4$ |
   | `king` | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0.5 | 0 |
   | `queen` | 0 | 1 | 1 | $-0.5$ | 0 |
   | `xqzv` | 0.2 | $-0.3$ | 0.1 | 0.3 | $-0.1$ |

3. Relabelling a vocabulary means permuting its words. Check that each of the $5! = 120$ relabellings of the one-hot vectors of @tbl-one-hot leaves the matrix of distances unchanged. Then exchange the labels `dawn` and `king` in the dense table of the previous question, so that each word receives the other's vector, and compare the distance between `dawn` and `dusk` before and after. What does the difference tell you about which of the two representations can contain meaning?
:::

One-hot vectors are equidistant, and equidistance is more than an inconvenience. It is the geometry of maximal ignorance, and it has four consequences, two of which the questions above probe. The first is that there is no such thing as "nearby". The nearest neighbours of `king` are all the other $|V|-1$ words, always at distance $\sqrt{2}$, so retrieval, clustering and similarity search have nothing to work with. This is the `LIKE '%monarch%'` wall of the previous section in geometric form.

The second consequence is that what is learned about one word does not transfer to similar words. A linear model reading a one-hot vector computes $\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{e}_i \rangle = w_i$, one independent parameter per word, so learning that "attack at dawn" is a military order tells it nothing about "attack at dusk", and a word that rarely appears gets a parameter that is barely trained.

The third is that the geometry is blind to renaming. Permuting the coordinates, which is the same as relabelling the words, preserves every distance. This is the vector form of the alpha-equivalence we met for programs, where renaming `customer_balance` to `x7` changes nothing. For a program that is a virtue, but for a human language it is fatal, because exchanging `dawn` and `dusk` *does* change what a sentence says.

Finally, the dimension grows with the vocabulary. A space of dimension $d$ contains at most $d$ mutually orthogonal non-zero vectors, so $|V|$ words forced to be orthogonal need $|V|$ dimensions. With a vocabulary of 50,000 words, each vector has 49,999 zeros and a single 1, and every new word adds a dimension to the space.

The flaw lies in the encoding, not in the learner, which is why more data or a bigger model does not repair it. If similarity is to exist, it must be built into the representation itself: each word needs a position in a space whose geometry is not the trivial one, so that `dawn` can lie close to `dusk` and far from `xqzv`. The way out is surprisingly simple. Multiplying the one-hot vector $\mathbf{e}_i$ by a matrix $\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d}$ with $d \ll |V|$ just selects its $i$-th row, a dense vector of $d$ real numbers, and if the rows are learned instead of fixed, they are free to move closer together or farther apart. That matrix is an **embedding**, and the rest of this chapter and book will revolve around how embeddings work and where their values come from.

But what if the symbolic world could be repaired from the inside, by defining exactly when two symbols *mean the same thing*, so that we could skip the geometry altogether? The next section shows why this cannot work, and why the graded notion of similarity that an embedding provides is not a luxury but the only option left.

## Rice's Theorem: Why Exact Meaning Is Out of Reach

Perhaps human language is too complex and nuanced, and meaning is easier to extract from formal languages. Could we simplify the problem by extracting meaning from the symbols of our beloved programming languages? For words, the equidistance of one-hot symbols is unacceptable, but programs have an advantage: their meaning is not vague. The meaning of a program is a mathematical object, a (partial) function that maps each input to the output of the program, or to nothing if it never halts. Perhaps we can repair the symbolic world from within, with no geometry at all, by writing a procedure that decides whether two programs have the same input-output behaviour, and therefore compute the same mathematical object, and grouping the programs accordingly. Take bubble sort and insertion sort. Their texts differ, so as symbols they are as far apart as `dawn` and `xqzv`, yet they compute the same function and any user would call them the same program. This is equality of *meaning*, of what a program does rather than how it is written, and it is exactly what Shannon left out by design and what the staircase does not measure. If it is possible to extract meaning from symbols anywhere, it is in the world of programming. Rice's theorem says that it cannot be done.

Rice's theorem [@rice1953classes], which generalizes Turing's halting problem [@turing1936computable], says that every interesting question about what a program does (that is, about the function it implements, its meaning), as opposed to what it looks like, is undecidable. Rice's insight is that this difficulty is not special to the halting problem---deciding whether a program stops or loops forever---but contaminates every question about the behaviour of programs.

It is fascinating how many of the familiar limitations in software engineering are this theorem in disguise. No static analyzer can promise to find every null-pointer dereference without raising false alarms, because "does this program ever dereference null?" is a question about behaviour. No antivirus can be perfect, because the author of the malware is free to choose a text that hides what it does. Tests can refute a program but never prove it correct: a failing test is a counterexample anyone can check, while a thousand passing ones leave open the thousand and first input. And a compiler will never turn bubble sort into insertion sort, let alone into merge sort. It cannot decide whether two programs are equivalent, so it applies a small library of rewrites, each proved safe in advance.

It would be a mistake to read the theorem as "nothing can be known about programs". It forbids a single procedure that is exact, general and always terminating, and almost every word in that sentence matters. It is silent about questions on the text: whether a program contains a `while` loop or has balanced brackets is settled by a parser, which is why everything in the Chomsky section remains valid. It is silent about questions that mention the clock: whether a program halts within 1,000 steps and prints 65 is settled by running it for 1,000 steps, because the bound limits the search. It is silent about weaker machines, those that are not Turing complete: whether two regular expressions accept the same strings is decidable, while the same question for two context-free grammars is not, so the staircase turns out to be a trade-off between expressiveness and the questions we are still allowed to ask. And it is silent about particular programs: bubble sort and insertion sort can be proved equivalent by hand, and verified compilers do this for every rewrite they perform. What no one can do is automate the proof for all programs. Even then, one side of the question stays open: if a program has the property and halts, running it will eventually confirm it, but for a program still running we can never get a firm "no".

So the hope of deciding meaning exactly from the text of a program is closed. Whatever notion of similar meaning we use for code has to be approximate and graded, a distance rather than an identity, and the raw material for it is the one-sided evidence we do have. Represent each program by what it does on a set of probe inputs, and the distance between two programs is how much their outputs differ on them. This is a first embedding of code, built from behaviour instead of text. Bubble sort and insertion sort become neighbours, and a positive distance is a proof of difference, but a zero distance proves nothing, as the last exercise below will show.

Just as the previous section associated vectors with words, we can associate numeric vectors with programs. In 2019, code2vec [@alon2019code2vec] was an early learned code embedding, placing snippets with similar behaviour close together, with no guarantee. Learned code embeddings have since been developed much further. These embeddings do not escape Rice's theorem; they trade the impossible exact answer for a useful graded one, and the price is certainty. The same trade-off will reappear for words: there is no table of exact meanings to look up, only positions in a space from which similarity can be read. What remains is to see how such positions are obtained, and the next section starts with the idea that made them practical: to stop describing a symbol by its identity and describe it by a pattern spread across many continuous dimensions.

::: {.questions}
1. Take this program, which counts how many steps the Collatz iteration needs to reach 1:

   ```python
   def steps(n):
       count = 0
       while n != 1:
           n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
           count += 1
       return count
   ```

   Ask an LLM what it does and what `steps(27)` returns, then run it to check. Write down which model you used and the date. Then keep varying the program and keep asking: rename the variables, replace the loop by recursion, add dead code, change `3 * n + 1` into `3 * n - 1`, and finally ask whether a program that tries the even numbers 4, 6, 8, ... and stops at the first one that is not the sum of two primes ever halts. How do you know when an answer is right? For each answer that is wrong or unsure, classify the failure: a limit of this model, which a better one might overcome, or a limit of the problem, which no model could overcome. Whatever your model answered, which variations fall in each class? If you found an LLM that always described correctly what a program does, would it disprove Rice's theorem?

2. In this exercise a program is a Python generator: it does one step of work each time it reaches a `yield`, and returns its result when it ends.

   ```python
   def quick():
       yield
       return 65

   def slow():
       for _ in range(5000):
           yield
       return 65

   def forever():
       while True:
           yield
   ```

   Write `check(program, budget)`, which runs a program for at most `budget` steps and returns `True` if it ends with the result 65, `False` if it ends with another result, and `None` ("unknown") if the budget runs out first. Try it on the three programs and on one of your own that returns 1, with budgets of 10 and 10,000. For which program does a larger budget change the answer? For the `forever` generator, does `check` ever stop answering `None`, however large the budget? Why can it not simply answer `False` after a very large number of steps?

3. Compare two ways of representing five programs: `bubble_sort`, `insertion_sort`, `sort_descending`, `identity` and `sort_unless_huge`, which sorts any list with fewer than 1,000 items and returns longer ones unchanged. In the first, each program is a symbol, a one-hot vector. In the second, it is the vector of its outputs on 30 random lists of 6 digits, concatenated. Compute the matrix of Euclidean distances for both representations. What does each say about `bubble_sort` and `insertion_sort`, and about `bubble_sort` and `sort_unless_huge`? Find an input that proves two of the programs different, and explain why a distance of zero between two programs proves nothing while a positive distance proves something. How does this connect to Rice's theorem?
:::

## Counting Company: Co-occurrence and Mutual Information

Both the Orthogonal Catastrophe and Rice's theorem expose the limits of one-hot representations: every symbol is equally far from every other, and exact meaning cannot be computed. The alternative is to describe a symbol by a pattern spread across many continuous dimensions. The idea is older than it looks. In 1986 Geoffrey Hinton contrasted two ways in which a neural network can represent concepts [@hinton1986learning]. In the *localist* representation each concept is a single unit, which is the one-hot vector under another name. In the *distributed* representation a concept is a pattern of activity over many units, and each unit takes part in many concepts. Its advantage, he argued, is automatic generalization: when the weights change to absorb something new about one concept, the change also affects every concept whose pattern is similar. This is the transfer that the one-hot model of the Orthogonal Catastrophe could not deliver and the dense vectors could, in exercise 2 of that section: `dusk` got a probability of 0.98 of being a time of day without ever appearing in the training set. Counting, the subject of this section, is the first step towards such patterns for words; the next section turns the counts into dense vectors.

For words we have a problem. The dense table of the Orthogonal Catastrophe was written by hand, by someone who already knew what `dawn` and `dusk` mean, which is a circular recipe, and no one can write one for 50,000 words. We need a source of meaning that requires no human annotator. Firth's slogan, "you shall know a word by the company it keeps", points to one, because company is something a machine can count.

Here is a toy world of thirteen sentences, laid out in two columns. Ten describe a sky and a court with queens and kings, and the last three contain the meaningless `xqzv` and a companion `jwk`, which stand only next to each other, to themselves and to `the`:

```
the dawn breaks over the hills      the king wears the crown
the dusk falls over the hills       the queen wears the crown
the dawn breaks over the sea        the king rules the land
the dusk falls over the sea         the queen rules the land
the dawn breaks over the sea        the king rules the land
the xqzv jwk                        the jwk xqzv jwk
the xqzv jwk jwk xqzv
```

Fix a window of one word on each side, and let $C_{wc}$ be the number of times the word $c$ appears immediately before or immediately after the word $w$, counting both sides together. Since the window is symmetric, $C_{wc} = C_{cw}$, and the matrix forgets the order: `the dawn` and `dawn the` add the same count. In a real language the left and right neighbours play different roles (an article comes before its noun, a verb after its subject), so merging them loses the direction. That matters for syntax but little for similarity, which is what we are after, and question 2 shows the cost; a richer model would count the two sides separately. Given the set $V$ of words, the result is a $|V| \times |V|$ matrix $\mathbf{C}$, of size $16 \times 16$ here, and the row of $w$ is a vector with one entry per word of the vocabulary: a profile of its neighbours, where the one-hot vector had a single 1 at the position of the word itself. @tbl-cooc shows the rows of five words, restricted to the six columns where any of them has a non-zero count.

| | `the` | `breaks` | `falls` | `wears` | `rules` | `jwk` |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `dawn` | 3 | 3 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `dusk` | 2 | 0 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `king` | 3 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| `queen` | 2 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| `xqzv` | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 5 |

: Rows of the co-occurrence matrix $\mathbf{C}$ for five words of the toy world. {#tbl-cooc}

The row of `dawn` has two non-zero entries, `breaks` (3 times) and `the` (3 times), and that of `dusk` has `falls` (2) and `the` (2). Their cosine similarity, the dot product of the two rows divided by the product of their lengths (the cosine of the angle between them: 1 if they point in the same direction, 0 if they are orthogonal, and never negative for counts, which cannot be negative), is $6/(\sqrt{18}\sqrt{8}) = 0.50$, all of it contributed by `the`. The first column of @tbl-counting, further below, gives the cosine of four pairs of words. Raw counts get `king` and `queen` right (0.98), but they put `dawn` closer to `king` (0.57) than to `dusk` (0.50), and even give it some similarity to the meaningless `xqzv` (0.26). The culprit is `the`, which stands next to everything, so that sharing it says almost nothing.

Raw counts fail because they ignore how common each neighbour is. Shannon's tools measure this directly. Pick at random one of the pairs counted in $\mathbf{C}$, a word $w$ and one of its neighbours $c$. The surprisal of each word alone is $-\log_2 P(w)$ and $-\log_2 P(c)$ bits, and that of the pair is $-\log_2 P(w,c)$. If the two words were independent, entropies would add, as in the first section, and the pair would cost exactly the sum of its parts. The **pointwise mutual information** (PMI) is the difference, the number of bits saved by naming the pair together instead of its two words separately:

$$
\mathrm{PMI}(w,c) = -\log_2 P(w) - \log_2 P(c) + \log_2 P(w,c) = \log_2 \frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)\,P(c)}.
$$

It is zero if the pair appears exactly as often as independent words would produce it, positive if the words attract each other, and negative if they avoid each other. In our world, `dawn` and `breaks` cost 4.17 and 4.17 bits separately but only 5.17 bits as a pair: 3.17 bits saved. `dawn` and `the` cost 4.17 and 1.71 bits separately and the same 5.17 bits as a pair: 0.71 bits saved. Averaged over all the pairs, weighted by $P(w,c)$, the saving is Shannon's **mutual information** between a word and its neighbour, $I(W;W') = H(W) + H(W') - H(W,W')$, which is zero exactly when the entropies add, that is, when neighbours are independent of words. We need only the value for a single pair, which Church and Hanks used to find word associations for lexicography [@church1990word].

The true probabilities are unknown, but we can estimate them by the relative frequencies in the corpus. Let $N = \sum_{w,c} C_{wc}$ be the total number of pairs. The estimates are

$$
\hat{P}(w,c) = \frac{C_{wc}}{N}, \qquad \hat{P}(w) = \frac{\sum_c C_{wc}}{N}, \qquad \hat{P}(c) = \frac{\sum_w C_{wc}}{N},
$$

where the marginals are the sums of the rows and the columns of the matrix, divided by $N$. From here on, $\mathrm{PMI}(w,c)$ means the value obtained by plugging these estimates into the formula. The estimates are reliable for frequent pairs and noisy for rare ones, which matters below.

In our world `dawn` stands next to `breaks` nine times more often than chance, $\mathrm{PMI} = \log_2 9 = 3.17$ bits, but next to `the` only 1.64 times more often, 0.71 bits. A pair that never occurs has $\mathrm{PMI} = -\infty$, and a negative value estimated from a handful of counts is hardly more reliable, so the usual remedy is to keep only the positive evidence, the **positive PMI** (PPMI), $\mathrm{PPMI}(w,c) = \max(0, \mathrm{PMI}(w,c))$.

| Pair | Counts | PPMI |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| `dawn`–`dusk` | 0.50 | 0.04 |
| `king`–`queen` | 0.98 | 0.98 |
| `dawn`–`king` | 0.57 | 0.05 |
| `dawn`–`xqzv` | 0.26 | 0.00 |

: Cosine similarity of four pairs of words in the toy world, for raw counts and for PPMI. {#tbl-counting}

The second column of @tbl-counting shows the effect. The pull of `the` is gone, and `dawn` is no longer close to `king` (0.05). But `dawn` and `dusk` have also drifted apart (0.04), because they never stand next to the same informative word: one is followed by `breaks` and the other by `falls`. We have reweighted the counts and kept the geometry of the one-hot vectors, rows that are long, sparse and nearly orthogonal. Yet `dawn` and `dusk` should be alike, since both appear in the same kind of sentence. What can we do to fix this? 

::: {.questions}
1. Using the thirteen sentences of this section, build the co-occurrence matrix with a window of one word and the PPMI matrix with `numpy`, and reproduce @tbl-counting. Print the rows of `dawn` and `dusk` of $\mathbf{C}$ and compute $\mathrm{PMI}(\text{dawn}, \text{breaks})$ and $\mathrm{PMI}(\text{dawn}, \text{the})$ by hand. Which pair does PPMI fail to bring together, and why?

2. Download a book as plain text from the Internet (for example, from Project Gutenberg) and count its co-occurrences with a window of one word, as in this section. Use the estimates $\hat{P}(w,c)$ to generate text as a Markov chain: starting from a word $w$, draw the next word $c$ with probability $\hat{P}(c \mid w) = \hat{P}(w,c)/\hat{P}(w)$, then continue from $c$. Generate thirty words. Then count only the word that *follows* each word, as in the $n = 1$ model of the exercise in Shannon's Boundary Problem, and generate thirty words again. Which text reads better, and what does the difference say about what the matrix $\mathbf{C}$ has lost?
:::

## From Counting to Geometry

The PPMI matrix of the previous section keeps `dawn` and `dusk` apart because one is followed by `breaks` and the other by `falls`. @tbl-cooc-over shows the rows of that matrix for these two words and for `breaks` and `falls`, restricted to the six columns where any of them is non-zero:

| | `the` | `breaks` | `falls` | `dawn` | `dusk` | `over` |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `dawn` | 0.71 | 3.17 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `dusk` | 0.71 | 0 | 3.75 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `breaks` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 3.17 | 0 | 2.43 |
| `falls` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 3.75 | 2.43 |

: Rows of the PPMI matrix $\mathbf{M}$ for `dawn`, `dusk`, `breaks` and `falls`, in bits. Zeros are pairs that never occur. {#tbl-cooc-over}

The rows of `dawn` and `dusk` share only `the`, which has a small value, and they are kept apart by two columns: `dawn` stands next to `breaks` and `dusk` next to `falls`. But those two columns are not completely unrelated. The rows of `breaks` and `falls` are different, because one word stands next to `dawn` and the other next to `dusk`, but both stand next to `over` (e.g., `the dawn breaks over the hills` and `the dusk falls over the hills`), so they play the same role, and their cosine is 0.33. If `breaks` and `falls` counted as the same coordinate, `dawn` and `dusk` should be alike. But whether they are alike depends on whether `breaks` and `falls` are, and the reverse. How can a method discover all of this at once?

Think of the rows of the PPMI matrix $\mathbf{M}$ as a data set with one point per word: the row $\mathbf{m}_w$ tells how $w$ combines with each of the $|V|$ context words. The PMI of a pair tells us whether two words keep each other's company, and `dawn` and `dusk` never do. Instead, we can compare whether the two words have the same companions, that is, how both combine with all the other words, which is what the cosine of their rows does. But it does so coordinate by coordinate, and the coordinates `breaks` and `falls` are as unrelated as two axes of a one-hot vector: `dawn` is large on one, `dusk` on the other, and their cosine is 0.04. We need coordinates in which `breaks` and `falls` count as the same thing.

There is also a practical reason. With a vocabulary of 50,000 to 100,000 words, each word has 50,000 to 100,000 coordinates, and we would like to keep only $d \ll |V|$ of them. We can get both goals by changing coordinates and then dropping some of them. Changing coordinates means choosing a new orthonormal basis of **patterns**, unit vectors that mix many context words, and describing each word by its coordinates along them. This loses nothing: it is a rotation, and all dot products, distances and cosines stay the same, because the dot product of two rows is the sum, over the patterns, of the products of their coordinates. Dropping coordinates, keeping only those along the first $d$ patterns, is the step that loses, and the only one that changes distances: it removes the terms of that sum that belong to the other patterns. So everything depends on which patterns we keep.

Which $d$ patterns should we keep? The ones that distort the rows the least. Replace each row $\mathbf{m}_w$ by its projection on the subspace spanned by the patterns, and measure the damage by the reconstruction error, the sum over all words of the squared distance between a row and its projection:

$$
\min_{\mathbf{V}_d} \sum_w \bigl\| \mathbf{m}_w - \mathbf{V}_d \mathbf{V}_d^\top \mathbf{m}_w \bigr\|^2,
$$

where $\mathbf{V}_d$ has $d$ orthonormal columns, the patterns, and $\mathbf{V}_d \mathbf{V}_d^\top \mathbf{m}_w$ is the projection of $\mathbf{m}_w$. This is the optimization problem of **principal component analysis** (PCA). By Pythagoras, the squared length of a row is the squared length of its projection plus that of the remainder, so the problem has an equivalent reading: find the subspace on which the projected words keep as much of the total squared length, the spread of the data, as possible.

The **singular value decomposition** (SVD) is the algorithm that solves it. It factors the matrix as $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\top$, where $\mathbf{U}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ have orthonormal columns and $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ is diagonal, with entries $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge 0$ called the **singular values**. The solution has four main properties. First, the columns of $\mathbf{V}$ are the patterns, orthogonal to each other and ordered by importance, so that the best subspace of dimension $d$ is spanned by the first $d$ of them. Second, the solutions are nested: we compute the decomposition once and then choose $d$ afterwards. It is not obvious that picking the patterns one at a time, each the best given the previous ones, gives the best subspace overall, but the Eckart–Young theorem [@eckart1936approximation, pp. 211-218] proves that it does. Third, the squares $\sigma_k^2$ say how much of the total squared length the $k$-th pattern keeps, so the reconstruction error of keeping $d$ patterns is exactly $\sum_{i>d} \sigma_i^2$, and the decay of the singular values tells how much a given $d$ costs. Fourth, the coordinates of the words along the patterns are the rows of $\mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Sigma}$, since $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Sigma}$; keeping the first $d$ gives the best rank-$d$ approximation $\mathbf{M}_d = \mathbf{U}_d \mathbf{\Sigma}_d \mathbf{V}_d^\top$ of the matrix.

One caveat: PCA proper subtracts the mean of each column first, and then the $\sigma_k^2$ are proportional to variances. We do not, because PPMI has a natural zero, no association, that centring would move (on our toy world it would lower the cosine of `dawn` and `dusk` from 1.00 to 0.36 at $d = 5$). The decomposition does not need to be invented for words: Deerwester and colleagues had applied it to the matrix of words by documents in 1990 and called it latent semantic indexing [@deerwester1990indexing].

Take $\mathbf{M}$ to be the PPMI matrix and define

$$
\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{U}_d \mathbf{\Sigma}_d \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d}.
$$

The row of a word in $\mathbf{E}$ lists its coordinates along the $d$ strongest patterns. This is the matrix $\mathbf{E}$ of the Orthogonal Catastrophe, whose rows are the embeddings, with one difference: nobody chose its values. Since $\mathbf{E}\mathbf{E}^\top = \mathbf{M}_d \mathbf{M}_d^\top$, the dot product of two embeddings is the dot product of the corresponding rows of the best rank-$d$ approximation of $\mathbf{M}$, so two words are close when the same $d$ patterns explain their neighbours. The second column of @tbl-svd is the result for $d = 5$: `dawn` and `dusk` have a cosine of 1.00, `king` and `queen` 1.00, and `dawn` is far from `king` and from the meaningless `xqzv`. The mechanism is the one we guessed: in the same embedding, `breaks` and `falls` have a cosine above 0.99.

What does the compression leave out? In our toy world the fourth pattern is the court (`wears` and `rules` against `king` and `queen`) and the fifth is the nonsense pair `xqzv`–`jwk`, while the first three mix sky and court words. On all five, `dawn` and `dusk` have coordinates of the same sign, and so do `breaks` and `falls`. What tells them apart are the sixth and seventh patterns, where their coordinates have opposite signs, and $d=5$ stops just before them. The difference between dawn and dusk is real, but it ranks below the patterns that organize the whole corpus.

| Pair | PPMI | SVD, $d=5$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| `dawn`–`dusk` | 0.04 | **1.00** |
| `king`–`queen` | 0.98 | **1.00** |
| `dawn`–`king` | 0.05 | 0.09 |
| `dawn`–`xqzv` | 0.00 | 0.00 |

: Cosine similarity of the same four pairs of words, for the PPMI matrix and for its rank-5 SVD embeddings. {#tbl-svd}

The dimension $d$ is a dial, and it is easy to see what happens at both ends. With $d = 1$ every word is described by its position along the dominant pattern and the sky and court words look alike, even `dawn` and `king`. At $d = 2$ the cosine between them is still 0.59, and from $d = 3$ to $d = 5$ it stays between 0.09 and 0.13, while that of `dawn` and `dusk` remains at 1.00. Beyond that, the extra directions are spent on the remaining differences between the two words: at $d = 6$ the cosine drops to 0.48, at $d = 8$ to 0.04, and at $d = 12$, the rank of this matrix, we recover the PPMI matrix exactly, and with it all its distinctions. Low rank is not a compromise that we accept to save memory; it is the mechanism. Compression forces the model to find what the rows have in common, and what they have in common is what generalizes.

The same recipe works on a real text, with three choices that Levy and colleagues showed to matter for it [@levy2015improving]. We counted the neighbours within a window of two words, which they found PPMI and SVD to prefer to longer ones, of the 2,000 most frequent words of *Pride and Prejudice* (about 128,000 words). We computed the PPMI smoothing the distribution of contexts, raising their counts to the power 0.75, which lowers the bonus that rare contexts receive. And we scaled the directions by the square root of the singular values, $\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{U}_d \mathbf{\Sigma}_d^{1/2}$, instead of by the singular values themselves, the traditional weighting that we used on the toy world and that they found to perform much worse on similarity benchmarks. We kept $d = 30$ dimensions. The nearest neighbours of `sister` are `father`, `daughter`, `mother`, `cousin`, `aunt`, `friend` and `uncle`; those of `morning` are `day`, `evening`, `next` and `week`; and those of `darcy` are `bingley`, `bennet` and `wickham`. Nobody told the method what a sister or a morning is. The neighbours of `darcy` also show what kind of similarity this is: not synonymy, but sharing a role, here that of a character who is spoken about and speaks in the same kind of sentences. Distributional similarity mixes substitutability and association, and a model of meaning built on it will inherit both.

This is a first embedding that was computed rather than written, and it comes with the costs of its method. The matrix $\mathbf{C}$ has up to $|V|^2$ entries, ten billion for a vocabulary of 100,000 words. Most of them are zero, but the SVD needs the whole matrix before it can start, so that new text means starting again. None of these costs concerns the quality of the vectors; they concern scale. The hand-written table of the Orthogonal Catastrophe could not scale to 50,000 words, and the factorization of a complete matrix does not scale to the text of the web. Richard Sutton gave this pattern a name, the *bitter lesson* [@sutton2019bitter]: in the long run, general methods that keep improving as more computation becomes available beat methods that build in what researchers know, however satisfying the second kind feels. The lesson is about how an algorithm uses computation, not about the shape of the model: the winning method is sometimes simple and sometimes linear, and sometimes neither. We will keep returning to it, and in this chapter it explains the next step. In the next section we meet a family of models that never build this matrix. They walk through the text and learn to predict, and, as we will see, what they end up computing is very close to the matrix we have just factored.

::: {.questions}
1. Take the PPMI matrix of the thirteen sentences and compute its SVD with `numpy`. Reproduce the second column of @tbl-svd with $d = 5$. Then check the claim that `breaks` and `falls` become similar: what is their cosine in the PPMI matrix and in the embeddings with $d = 5$?

2. Repeat the experiment on a real book: take the 2,000 most frequent words, count the neighbours within a window of two words, compute the PPMI with the context distribution raised to the power 0.75, and factor it with $d = 30$. For `sister`, `morning`, `darcy` and `london`, list the nearest neighbours by cosine in three representations: raw counts, PPMI and SVD. Which representation gives the cleanest lists, which words in them are not similar in meaning, and why?

3. Compute the Frobenius error $\|\mathbf{M} - \mathbf{M}_d\|_F$ of the truncated SVD of the toy PPMI matrix for $d = 1, \dots, 8$ and check that it equals $\sqrt{\sum_{i>d}\sigma_i^2}$. Compare it with the error of rank-$d$ approximations obtained by projecting the columns of $\mathbf{M}$ onto random $d$-dimensional subspaces. Then print the cosine of `dawn` and `dusk` for each $d$ next to the error. Does a smaller error always give a better embedding?
:::

## Learning by Prediction

*Plan (3–4 pages).* Word2Vec skip-gram with negative sampling, told as history (2013): predict the context of a word and minimize a cross-entropy, Shannon's second quantity. Levy and Goldberg's result [@levy2014neural] that SGNS implicitly factors the shifted PMI matrix of the last two sections, so counting and predicting are two routes to the same geometry. The bitter lesson in its first concrete form: streaming stochastic gradient descent over the text scales where a full factorization of $\mathbf{C}$ does not, and @levy2015improving found that, with the same hyperparameters, count-based methods close much of the gap. What prediction bought was scale and convenience, not a different geometry. One paragraph on GloVe as the explicit regression on log co-occurrences [@pennington2014glove], and one pointing to Chapter 4 for contextual embeddings, where the vector of a word depends on its sentence. Exercises: train a tiny SGNS model and compare its vectors with the SVD ones.

## Learning by Contrast

*Plan (3 pages).* InfoNCE: pull positive pairs together and push negatives apart, a lower bound on mutual information, Shannon's third quantity. The temperature $\tau$ as the dial between easy and hard negatives. Wang and Isola's decomposition into alignment and uniformity on the hypersphere [@wang2020understanding]. Connect back to the behavioural embedding of programs in the Rice exercises: two programs that agree on the probes are a positive pair. The pattern is contrastive learning with negatives, and InfoNCE is the instance that made it standard; CLIP is one dated application, not the lesson. The bitter lesson again: no one writes the similarity table, because the data supplies the positive pairs and the batch supplies the negatives, so the method improves as data and compute grow. This is the objective behind the sentence embeddings used for retrieval in Chapter 3. Exercise: contrastive training of program or sentence embeddings on a toy set.

## The Geometry of Meaning

*Plan (3–4 pages).* On the unit sphere cosine similarity and Euclidean distance carry the same information, $\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|_2^2 = 2 - 2\cos\theta$; the direction of a vector encodes its category and its norm encodes frequency and salience. Mikolov's analogy parallelogram, $\mathbf{v}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{v}_{\text{woman}} \approx \mathbf{v}_{\text{queen}}$ [@mikolov2013efficient], and why it follows from ratios of co-occurrence probabilities becoming differences of logarithms [@arora2016latent; @pennington2014glove]. A brief note on steering vectors: the same linear structure, found inside the activations of modern LLMs, and developed in Chapter 4 as the linear representation hypothesis. Keep three claims apart: that dot products are what hardware computes cheaply (why linear read-outs scale), that concepts are directions in learned spaces (an empirical claim about what training finds), and the bitter lesson (a claim about methods, which does not say that the winner is linear). Exercise: test analogies on pre-trained vectors and find where they fail.

## Where a Single Vector Strains

*Plan (2–3 pages).* Anisotropy: trained embeddings crowd into a narrow cone, so that all cosines are high, and the simple remedies of centering and whitening. Hubness, a few points that are the nearest neighbour of almost everything, as a first sign of the strangeness of high dimensions studied in Chapter 2. Close with, in prose, the ledger of limits that the rest of the book examines. Each is stated as a cost, not as an impossibility, and each says whether it is structural or contingent: a nearest-neighbour query cannot negate or chain, and a fixed-dimension dot product can realize only a limited family of rankings (Chapter 3); flat space needs more dimensions than curved space to hold a hierarchy at the same distortion (Chapter 5); symmetric dot products cannot express asymmetric relations (Chapter 6); pairwise structure does not directly encode multi-way interactions (Chapter 7); similarity alone is not a logic, because negation and conjunction need more than a score (Chapter 8); a sum of vectors cannot say which attribute belongs to which object, the binding problem (Chapter 9); systematic composition is the open question of Chapter 10; and the coordinates of a trained space are arbitrary up to an isometry, so comparing two spaces is a problem of its own (Chapter 11). End on the other side of the ledger: the thesis is not that a single vector fails and a richer geometry repairs it, but that a single vector is a strong first answer and every extension is a trade. For each limit the question is whether more dimensions, data and compute substitute for the added structure, which is the bitter lesson applied to geometry.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Further Reading {.unnumbered}

Counting, predicting and contrasting are not unrelated techniques but convergent estimators of the same co-occurrence statistics. @levy2014neural shows that the predictive Word2Vec objective is an implicit factorization of a shifted PMI matrix, @arora2016latent develops the latent-variable argument for why PMI-based factorization and log-bilinear regression agree, and @pennington2014glove derives the GloVe objective in full. @sutton2019bitter is a short statement of the pattern that this chapter traces from counting to predicting to contrasting. The next chapter's argument about embedding dimensionality rests on the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma [@johnson1984extensions, pp. 189-206], which bounds how much a point set can be projected into lower dimensions while approximately preserving pairwise distances.
